title: TB9-07052
frame:
Forum: Refugee Appeal Division (appeal tribunal).
Parties: the appellant and the Minister; names are redacted.
How the layers nest here: The RAD member is the author (layer 1). The appellant and the Minister make submissions to the RAD (layer 2). The RPD decision under appeal is layer 3, and what the claimant or the Minister said to the RPD, as reported, is layer 4.

paragraphs.text: XXXX XXXX XXXX (Principal Appellant) and XXXX XXXX XXXX (Associate Appellant), citizens of Nigeria, appealed a decision of the Refugee Protection Division (RPD), dated February 15, 2019, rejecting their claims for refugee protection.

The determinative issue on the appeal is credibility. The Principal Appellant alleges that her paternal family intends to forcibly initiate her to assume her birthright as the priest of the "XXXX XXXX" cult in Osun, Ekiti State. The RPD rejected her claim, citing credibility concerns as related to her lack of knowledge of the Orisa Ewu cult, discrepancies between two copies of her husband's affidavit, and a significant omission from her BOC. The RPD also found that the claim lacked an objective basis. The Principal Appellant challenges this decision, submitting that the RPD incorrectly impugned her credibility and determined that her claim did not have an objective basis.

As will be explained below, I do not find any error in the RPD's determination. In my own independent analysis, I find significant credibility concerns on the record. Furthermore, I agree with the RPD's finding that the claim lacks an objective basis. Consequently, the appeal is dismissed.

The following allegations are summarized in the Appellants' Basis of Claim forms (BOC)1 and oral testimony2. In brief, the Principal Appellant alleges that she was expected to assume the duty of priest of the XXXX XXXX cult, following the death of her father on XXXX XXXX, 2018. The Principal Appellant was visiting family in the United States of America when her father passed. The Principal Appellant's mother contacted her following her father's death, advising her not to return to Nigeria, for if she did, she would face forcible initiation to become the new priest of the cult. The Principal Appellant does not want to assume the role of priest, citing reasons that she is a Christian and that the cult engages in "barbaric practices" including restricting freedom of movement.

The Principal Appellant also claims that members of the XXXX XXXX threatened to kidnap her daughter (Associate Appellant) if she did not assume her role as priest. Following this threat, her daughter travelled to the United States in XXXX 2018. The Appellants then travelled together to Canada, crossing the border irregularly and making a claim for refugee protection on May 17, 2018.

The Principal Appellant submits no new evidence but has requested an oral hearing. As there was no new evidence submitted, pursuant to subsection 110(6) of IRPA, the RAD may not hold a hearing. Therefore, the application for an oral hearing is denied. The Appellant requests that the RAD substitutes a positive determination, or in the alternative, remits the matter to a newly constituted panel of the RPD for redetermination.

The Refugee Appeal Division (RAD) reviews decisions of the RPD on a standard of correctness after conducting an independent assessment of the evidence before it.3 The exception to this rule is where the RPD enjoys a meaningful advantage in the assessment and weighing of oral testimony heard, which, in particular cases, may attract deference. Unless specifically stated below, I have applied a correctness standard.

The following issues are determinative of the appeal: a. The RPD's conclusion there the Objective Basis for the Claim is not established is correct; b. The RPD's conclusion that the Principal Appellant lacks credibility is correct. Specifically: i. The Principal Appellant's affidavit was altered after it was sealed and signed by the Commissioner of Oaths and is, therefore, not credible evidence; ii. The Principal Appellant has not made any submissions regarding the omission of her family's loss of kingship from her BOC form, which undermines her credibility; and iii. The Principal Appellant demonstrated limited knowledge of the XXXX XXXX cult, which negatively impacts her credibility. c. The RPD did not fail to assess section 97. The RPD did not err when it found that the Objective Basis for the Claim is not established The Principal Appellant's Argument

The RPD relied upon the Response to Information Request (RIR) NGA103485.E, Nigeria: Consequences for a person to refuse a chief priest or fetish priest position for which they have been selected in south and central Nigeria to determine that the Principal Appellant's claim had no objective basis. The RPD noted that professors from the African Studies Centre (ASC) of the University of Leiden and the University of London did not believe that there would be consequences for someone who refuses to assume their role as chief priest. The RPD discounted the opinion of a Professor of Anthropology at the Southern Illinois University (SIU) who indicated that "in many communities it would be considered a 'big problem'"4 because the statement appeared vague, and the professor's research was based in a different geographic location than the town of Osun.

The Principal Appellant submits that there is no rational basis for the RPD to prefer the academic opinion of the professors from the Universities of London and Leiden to that of the professor from SIU. She submits that there is an objective basis for her fear. The RAD's Analysis

The RPD did not err when it found that the Principal Appellant had no objective basis for her fear. While the RPD/1 could have been more explicit in its explanation for its preference of academic opinion, my independent analysis yields the same result.

I do not prefer the opinion of the SIU Professor for the following reasons. First, like the RPD, I find the assertion that many communities would consider it a "big problem" if someone were to refuse to take on an inherited role as a shine priest to be vague. This statement does not describe any possible consequences for the decision to refuse this role. The definition of a "big problem" is left to subjective interpretation without specific examples or context.

Second, the full quotation from the RIR reads: The SIU Professor wrote that in many communities it would be considered "a big problem" if someone refused to take on the inherited role of shrine priest (3 June 2010). The SIU Professor further said people would believe that the individual was inviting "divine wrath" on themselves, as well as on the local community (3 June 2010).5 [Emphasis Added]

In reading the full excerpt, it appears that the "big problem" to which the SIU Professor is referring is limited to divine wrath. The professor does not explicitly state that the perception of divine wrath brought forth on a community could escalate to violence, and to make this conclusion would amount to speculation.

I prefer the opinions of the other interviewed academics for the following reasons. First, the opinions presented are specific, citing examples and detailing reasons for why it would not be considered an offence for someone to refuse the role of chief priest. The ASC Professor stated that he had "never heard of the priesthood being forced on anyone in Nigeria," indicating that communities prefer successors with an interest of aptitude for the role.6 The University of London Professor also indicated that there are "no consequences for someone who refuses a position as chief priest", citing the fact that Christians have been known to refuse the roles in shrines since the middle of the 19th century.7 When contrasted with the opinion of the SIU professor, I find these statements to be grounded in fact and supported by evidence, as opposed to the ambiguous statement of the SIU Professor.

Additionally, I note that a fourth professor from Franklin & Marshall College opined that individuals were only forced into these roles "in the old days."8 Like the SIU Professor, he also went on to state that the consequences for refusing to assume a role as priest are divine in nature: "there are people who maintain their ties to indigenous religion who swear that the shrine deities will find a way to punish those who refuse this."9 Therefore, although two of the four experts interviewed indicated the possibility of negative consequences for those who refuse to assume the role of chief priest, these negative opinions both appear to refer to divine rather than familial or community-based consequences.

In sum, after a review of the expert opinions on the matter, I do not find that the documentary evidence suggests that the Principal Appellant faces a serious possibility of persecution from her family due to her refusal to assume her role as chief priest of the XXXX XXXX cult. The claim therefore lacks an objective basis. At best, in the absence of any of the credibility problems outlined in my analysis below, it is possible that the members of the cult may believe that the Principal Appellant could be subject to divine consequences, rather than physical harm at the hands of her family. This assertion alone would not be enough to substantiate the Principal Appellant's objective basis for her fear of persecution. The Principal Appellant's affidavit was altered after it was sealed and signed by the Commissioner of Oaths and is therefore not credible evidence The Principal Appellant's Argument

The RPD noted that two different versions of her husband's affidavit were present in the record. The first affidavit contained a typographical error, stating "That XXXX XXXX is the deity workshop by her forefathers... [Emphasis added]"10, while the second version stated "That XXXX XXXX is the deity worshipped by her forefathers. [Emphasis added]"11 The version with the typographical error also was not signed by the deponent, while the second version was. All other elements of the document appear to be the same, including the dates, stamps, seals and signature of the Commissioner of Oaths.

The RPD noted that the affidavit appeared to have been changed after the Commissioner of Oaths stamped the document, and determined that the second page with the additional signature appeared to have been repurposed for use in the second version of the document. As a result, the RPD found that the affidavit was not reliable or trustworthy evidence, and gave it no weight. In conjunction with its other findings, the RPD found that this undermined the Principal Appellant's overall credibility.

The Principal Appellant argues that she was not canvassed as to how the second version of her husband's affidavit was sworn. She submits that, in any case, she would not have been able to speculate as to the process. The Principal Appellant submits that there were no material differences between the two documents. The Principal Appellant argues that the RPD engaged in speculation and conjecture when it opined that the affidavit was changed after the Commissioner of Oaths stamps and signature were affixed to the document and that there was no basis for this determination. The RAD's Analysis
The RPD did not err in its analysis of the affidavit for the following reasons.

First, although the RPD did not directly ask Principal Appellant how the second version of the document was sworn, the member provided the Principal Appellant with multiple opportunities to explain why the discrepancies occurred. The RPD included open-ended questions, such as "why are these different? Do you know?"12 and "What happened with this? Do you know what your husband did? Can you explain the difference in the affidavits?"13 When the Principal Appellant was evasive, the member posed follow-up questions, such as "Can you explain?"14 Furthermore, given that there were two versions of the document on the record, it was not an error for the RPD to expect the Principal Appellant to be able to provide an explanation as to the source of their differences. Finally, I note that the Principal Appellant has not put forth any further or alternative explanation as to how the two different versions of the document were produced and sworn. It is reasonable to expect that even if the Principal Appellant was unaware of the process of the swearing of the affidavit at the time of the hearing, she could have asked her husband for a fulsome explanation to include with her appeal. I find that the lack of further explanation negatively impacts the Principal Appellant's credibility.

Second, although the differences in document content are limited to a typographical error and a signature, the fact remains that the affidavit was clearly altered after the Commissioner of Oaths affixed a seal and signature to the document. I find no merit in the Principal Appellant's argument that the RPD did not have a basis in its finding that the affidavit was altered. In examining both versions of the affidavits on their face, it is clear that both documents appear to have identical seals, stamps and dates. The Principal Appellant testified that she "told him there are typographical errors in them that he should correct it."15 Counsel also testified that the affidavit was "redone."16 I therefore find sufficient evidence to determine that it is more likely than not that the affidavit was altered after the Commissioner of Oaths stamped and signed the document.

In this sense, it appears that the process of providing evidence was disrupted. Affidavits are sworn before a Commissioner of Oaths and sealed in order to attest to the fact that the content of the document is true and has not been altered. The fact that the seal appears to have been affixed prior to the finalization of the document disrupts the process of evidence to such a degree that I am unable to rely on the contents of the document as credible evidence. The degree of difference between the two versions of the affidavit is irrelevant; the issue at hand is the lack of credibility of either version of the document. Therefore, on a balance of probabilities, I am unable to accept the information in either version of the Principal Appellant's husband's affidavit as credible evidence and consequently ascribe it no weight in my independent analysis. I also find that the submission of a document that shows obvious signs of alteration disrupts the evidentiary process to the degree that the Principal Appellant's overall credibility is undermined. The Principal Appellant has not made any submissions regarding the omission of her family's loss of kingship from her BOC form, which undermines her credibility The RAD's Analysis

The Principal Appellant testified that she is under additional familial pressure, as her refusal to assume her role as priest of the XXXX XXXX will also result in her family's loss of the right to bid for the position of king of the town of Osun.17 The Principal Appellant did not include this detail in her BOC narrative. The RPD noted this omission, observing that the only corroborating source for this information appeared in the Principal Appellant's husband's affidavit, which it did not find to be trustworthy. The Principal Appellant's explanation for the omission was that she was unaware of this information until her father died in January 2018. The RPD did not find this explanation to be satisfactory, as the Principal Appellant's BOC form was signed May 23, 2018, following her father's death.

Although the Principal Appellant has not submitted any argument with respect to this finding, I find it important to address this significant omission. In my independent review of the record, I note the same omission, and do not find the Principal Appellant's explanation to be sufficient. As I also do not find the Principal Appellant's husband's affidavit to be credible evidence, I find nothing else on the record to support this element of the claim. I therefore find that the omission of this key detail and subsequent insufficient explanation diminish the claimant's overall credibility. The Principal Appellant demonstrated limited knowledge of the XXXX XXXX cult, which negatively impacts her credibility The Principal Appellant's Argument

The RPD found that the Principal Appellant's limited knowledge of the XXXX XXXX cult undermined her credibility. The RPD noted that the Principal Appellant went to live with her father in Osun, Ekiti State when he assumed the role of priest of the XXXX XXXX, where she remained for approximately six years. The RPD found it reasonable to expect that the Principal Appellant would have at least a basic knowledge of the cult, given the extended period of time she spent in close proximity to her father while he acted as chief. In concert with the other identified credibility concerns on the record, the RPD found that the Principal Appellant's rudimentary knowledge of the cult undermined her allegations that she would face persecution at the hands of her family for refusing to take on the role of chief priest.

The Applicant submits that it was unreasonable for the RPD to expect her to know and understand the details of the XXXX XXXX, especially in light of the alleged secrecy of the cult and the fact that she was raised as a Christian. The RAD's Analysis

In my independent analysis of the record, I find the following gaps in the Principal Appellant's knowledge of the XXXX XXXX cult: a. The Principal Appellant was unable to describe why her family worships or prays to the idol.18 b. The Principal Appellant was unable to describe the significance of the name "XXXX XXXX"19 c. The Principal Appellant could not coherently explain where or how her family worships the idol. First, she testified that her family worshipped and prayed to the idol "ìn a house."20 Later, she testified that "they don't really have a house that... but somebody have to pray, worship the deity on a weekly basis".21 d. The Principal Appellant could not describe the idol beyond a rough estimate of its size.22 The Principal Appellant explained that she was unable to describe the idol because the area where it is kept is dark. 23

I have considered the Principal Appellant's explanation for her lack of knowledge of the cult, and do not find it to be satisfactory. Although the Principal Appellant was raised as a Christian, I cannot ignore the Principal Appellant's testimony that she lived with her father while he assumed his duties as the head of the cult for approximately six years. I also note that the Principal Appellant testified that she has been aware of the cult since she was a child, as her family would travel home to see her grandfather while he allegedly held the role of chief priest. 24 In this regard, it appears more likely than not that the Principal Appellant would have a basic understanding of the cult and its background.

I have also considered the Principal Appellant's argument that the secretive nature of the cult may have prevented her from understanding its details. I find that the RPD did not expect the Principal Appellant to understand complex details such as rituals or ceremonies that would be understood through initiation and practice of the religion. Rather, the RPD questioned the Principal Appellant on basic principles of the cult and the behavior of its followers. I find that a close, non-practicing, uninitiated immediate family member of a cult leader would likely possess this knowledge.

When considered with other credibility concerns on the file, I find that the Principal Appellant's lack of knowledge of the basic details of the cult further impugns her credibility. The RPD did not fail to assess section 97 The Principal Appellant's Argument

The Principal Appellant argues that the RPD erred in failing to assess section 97 and cites two cases for this proposition, alleging that credibility is not necessarily determinative to the assessment under section 97.25 They also argue that "not having regard for the totality of the evidence is an error in law."26

The Principal Appellant alleges that the RPD erred when it "failed to consider the fact that removal of the applicants to their native Nigeria would subject them to risk of life or risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment as result of their being forced to take the position of the chief priest of the XXXX XXXX." The RAD's Analysis

First, I find that the RPD did not fail to assess section 97. I note that paragraphs 30 and 31 of the RPD decision clearly reference section 97. Although the reference is brief, I do not find that the RPD failed to turn its mind to section 97.

Second, the cited cases are distinguishable from the case at the bar. The Principal Appellant cites Ozdemir to illustrate the need to consider the facts of the case in a section 97 assessment. In Ozdemir, the RPD did not find the claimant, a Turkish citizen of Kurdish descent, to be credible in his claim that he was Kurdish. The RPD determined that he was of no interest to authorities except in regard to his possible military evasion. The Federal Court determined that the RPD ought to have more explicitly analyzed the prison conditions for military deserters in its decision. This case is distinguishable from the case at the bar in that the claimant presented an uncontested residual profile: that of a military deserter. I do not find any residual profile that arises out of the facts on the record in the case at hand.

In Bouaouni, although the Federal Court determined that the RPD committed a reviewable error by not specifically analyzing the section 97 claim, it also found that [A]part from the evidence that the Board found to be not credible, there was no other evidence before the board in the country documentation, or elsewhere, that could have led the Board to conclude that the applicant was a person in need of protection [Emphasis added].27

This conclusion is harmonious with other jurisprudence which places the onus on the Principal Appellant to produce independent and credible evidence capable of supporting a positive determination of the claim under section 97.28

The Principal Appellant has not established that there is any sort of independent or credible evidence capable of supporting a positive decision. There does not appear to be a residual claim linked to the specific circumstances of the claim. The Principal Appellant's argument that her potential to be forced to take the position of chief priest constitutes risk of life or cruel and unusual treatment or punishment only stands if these allegations are credible. In this instance, as outline above, the RPD correctly found that the Principal Appellant lacked credibility. Furthermore, as her allegations are inconsistent with the documentary evidence asserting that Nigerians do not face consequences for refusing a chief priest position, the Principal Appellant's claim lacks a credible basis.

In this appeal, credibility is central to all aspects of the threat of harm to the Appellants. Without credibility, a claim under s. 97 cannot stand. I therefore find that the RPD did not err in failing to assess section 97.

The RPD made a number of factual findings on the credibility of the Principal Appellant, which when examined cumulatively demonstrate that she lacks credibility. Consequently, her allegations are not established, on a balance of probabilities. The RPD also demonstrated that the Principal Appellant's claim lacked an objective basis. My independent analysis of the record yields the same results. I therefore find that the Appellant has not established that she had a faces a serious possibility of persecution in Nigeria due to her refusal to assume the role of chief priest of the XXXX XXXX cult.

The Associate Appellant's claim is directly linked to the allegations and credibility of the Principal Appellant. Given that the Principal Appellant's claim lacks both credibility and an objective basis, it follows that the Associate Appellant's claim must also fail.

The RAD dismisses the appeal and confirms the decision of the RPD that the Appellants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection, pursuant to section 111(1)(a) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).
